Blue-and-White Porcelain. A ceramic tradition featuring cobalt-blue decorations on white glazed backgrounds, originating in China and reaching its aesthetic and technical pinnacle during the Ming Dynasty from thirteen sixty-eight to sixteen forty-four. This style became the defining image of Chinese ceramics in the Western imagination and remains one of the world's most recognizable artistic traditions. The technique required advanced kiln technology and rare materials, making production a marker of imperial wealth and cultural refinement.

The tradition emerged during the Yuan Dynasty from twelve seventy-one to thirteen sixty-eight as Chinese artisans experimented with cobalt oxide imported from Persia. These early experiments produced modest quantities intended for elite consumption. The technique reached perfection during the Ming Dynasty under imperial patronage. Ming blue-and-white achieved unmatched quality and became the standard for imperial gifts and tribute items throughout Asia.

Cobalt oxide was the critical ingredient that made the process work. Imports from the Islamic world made production expensive and limited to court-sponsored kilns at Jingdezhen and other major ceramic centers. Common Ming motifs included dragons, phoenixes, flowers, landscapes, and calligraphic inscriptions. Decoration often featured naturalistic detail and narrative scenes that reflected the skill of individual artisans.

The Ming produced these ceramics in vast quantities during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, exporting them along the Silk Road to the Ottoman Empire, Persia, and eventually Europe, where they were prized as exotic luxury goods. European demand fueled a global trade network. Chinese porcelain influenced Western ceramics directly and led Europeans to attempt replicating the technique through the eighteenth century, though none matched the quality of the Ming originals.
